17	## The Governing Philosophy: Mechanistic Skeleton, Bayesian Flesh, and Graph Relationship Map
18	
19	The foundational design principle is that **every layer of the system is a mechanistic model with probability distributions on its parameters, not a black box**. Machine learning enters not to replace mechanism but to (a) extract and encode knowledge from literature and experiments, (b) serve as fast surrogates for expensive simulations, and (c) update parameter distributions as new evidence arrives. The result is a living, self-updating scientific belief system rather than a static model.
20	
21	Uncertainty is not an afterthought — it propagates upward through every layer, so that clinical predictions carry honest credible intervals that trace back to our ignorance about, say, a particular enzyme's Km in human sural nerve tissue.
22	
23	The relationships among all models — within layers and across layers — are captured in a **graph relationship map**. This is explicitly *not* a directed acyclic graph (DAG): the system contains feedback loops. Posterior updates from clinical outcomes propagate back to refine pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic parameters; tissue-level pathology constrains the gene-regulatory priors; virtual patient behavior feeds back into the biochemical kinetics of the next simulation cycle. A DAG cannot represent these cycles. The graph relationship map therefore uses a general directed graph, where nodes are model bundles and edges encode directional influence. This map serves as the connective tissue of the entire architecture: it determines which inferences must be recomputed when new evidence arrives, and it keeps the mechanistic structure explicit and auditable rather than buried in software dependencies.

158	---
159	
160	## Layered Architecture
161	
162	### Layer 1 — The Biochemical Core: Polyol Pathway Kinetics
163	
164	At the finest resolution, we build a fully parameterized ordinary differential equation model of the polyol pathway and its immediate consequences. Glucose enters via the aldose reductase (AKR1B1) reaction, producing sorbitol at the cost of NADPH; sorbitol dehydrogenase then oxidizes sorbitol to fructose at the cost of NAD⁺. These two reactions are the beating heart of the system, and their kinetics — Michaelis constants, catalytic rates, inhibition constants — are encoded as probability distributions, not point estimates.
165	
166	The model's state variables include intracellular glucose, sorbitol, fructose, NADPH/NADP⁺ ratio, and NAD⁺/NADH ratio. From these we derive downstream consequences that link to the next layer: depletion of NADPH starves glutathione reductase, reducing the GSH/GSSG ratio and driving oxidative stress; NADH accumulation feeds pseudohypoxia; elevated fructose fuels the hexosamine pathway and advanced glycation end-product (AGE) formation; and diacylglycerol accumulation activates protein kinase C isoforms. Each of these is itself a small mechanistic sub-module with its own parameterization.
167	
168	Bayesian priors for this layer come from decades of in vitro enzyme kinetics literature — Km and Vmax measured in crystallographic and biochemical studies, inhibition constants from aldose reductase inhibitor programs, and intracellular metabolite concentrations from isotope tracing experiments. A literature-mining AI agent (a fine-tuned large language model with structured extraction) continuously reads new papers and proposes updates to these priors, flagged for human scientist review before incorporation.
169	
170	---
171	
172	### Layer 2 — Gene Regulatory Networks: From Model Organisms to Humans
173	
174	The biochemical layer tells us what the pathway does given fixed enzyme levels, but gene expression is itself regulated and varies across individuals, tissues, and species. The second layer is a probabilistic gene regulatory network (GRN) model governing the expression of AKR1B1, SORD, and their transcriptional regulators — SP1, NF-κB, NRF2, and osmotic response element binding protein (OREBP/TonEBP), among others.
175	
176	In model organisms — primarily the streptozotocin rat and the db/db mouse — we have rich time-series transcriptomic data from sciatic and sural nerves under hyperglycemia, with and without aldose reductase inhibitor treatment. A Bayesian network learning algorithm (using a variant of the PC algorithm with Bayesian scoring) infers regulatory edges and assigns posterior probabilities to their existence and direction. The parameters of these regulatory relationships are themselves distributions, updated as new animal data arrive.
177	
178	The critical and most scientifically demanding step is species translation. Rodent and human AR gene promoters differ substantially; human GWAS and eQTL data from diabetic neuropathy cohorts (the DCCT/EDIC biorepository, UK Biobank, and others) are integrated as a separate data source. A hierarchical Bayesian model treats the rodent GRN and the human GRN as related but distinct, sharing structural priors while allowing divergence. Posterior inference on the human regulatory network is therefore informed by the richer rodent data but appropriately discounted. Genetic variants affecting AKR1B1 expression or enzyme function enter as modifiers of the prior, enabling patient stratification.
179	
180	---
181	
182	### Layer 3 — Cellular and Tissue Pathophysiology: The Neuron and Its Environment
183	
184	Peripheral sensory and motor neurons in diabetic neuropathy are damaged through a confluence of mechanisms that the polyol pathway feeds: oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired axonal transport, Schwann cell dysfunction, and endoneurial microvascular ischemia. Layer 3 translates the biochemical outputs of Layers 1–2 into cellular and tissue-level phenomena.
185	
186	Here we use a combination of mechanistic compartmental models and partial differential equations. Axonal transport is modeled as a reaction-diffusion system, with polyol pathway-driven ATP depletion and oxidative modification of kinesin/dynein motors entering as degradation terms — their magnitudes drawn from the distributions established in Layers 1 and 2. Mitochondrial membrane potential dynamics follow established biophysical frameworks (loosely in the Nicholls tradition), with ROS production coupled to the NADH/NAD⁺ imbalance from Layer 1. Nerve conduction velocity is an emergent output, computed from Hodgkin-Huxley-style cable models of myelinated axons with Schwann cell geometry parameterized from morphometric data in rodent and human nerve biopsy studies.
187	
188	Endoneurial blood flow is modeled as a separate but coupled sub-system: AGEs cross-link basement membrane components, nitric oxide synthesis is impaired through NADPH depletion, and the resulting ischemia feeds back on axonal oxygen availability. The coupling between vascular and neural sub-models is one of the richest sources of non-linearity — and therefore one of the most important contributors to uncertainty in downstream predictions.
189	
190	Because full simulation of this layer is computationally expensive, we train deep neural network surrogate models (emulators) that accept the parameter distributions from Layers 1–2 as inputs and return fast approximations of Layer 3 outputs with calibrated uncertainty. These emulators are retrained as new mechanistic simulations are run, in an active learning loop that prioritizes the parameter regions most relevant to clinical interventions being evaluated.
191	
192	---
193	
194	### Layer 4 — PK/PD Modeling: From Dose to Target Engagement
195	
196	This layer bridges pharmacology and mechanism. For any drug candidate — an aldose reductase inhibitor, an antioxidant, a PKC-β inhibitor, or a combination — we build a population pharmacokinetic model describing absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion, coupled to a pharmacodynamic model describing target engagement and downstream pathway modulation.
197	
198	The PD model is not an empirical Emax function but a direct interface to Layer 1: drug concentration in peripheral nerve tissue (a critical and poorly measured quantity in humans) inhibits the aldose reductase kinetic term, and the consequent changes in metabolite concentrations propagate through Layers 1–3 to produce predicted changes in nerve conduction velocity and biomarkers like nerve sorbitol content. PK/PD parameters in animal models are estimated from preclinical studies; allometric and mechanistic scaling rules (with Bayesian uncertainty) are used to project human PK from animal data. The historical failure of AR inhibitors in clinical trials — despite strong preclinical evidence — is directly encoded as a calibration dataset: the system must reproduce these null results at the appropriate human doses and exposures before it is trusted to predict new interventions.
199	
200	---
201	
202	### Layer 5 — Virtual Patient Modeling
203	
204	A virtual patient population is generated by sampling from the joint posterior distribution of patient-level parameters — baseline nerve conduction velocity, duration of diabetes, HbA1c trajectory, genetic variants affecting AKR1B1 expression, comorbidities affecting drug PK — yielding thousands of synthetic patients whose disease biology is governed by the mechanistic layers below.
205	
206	---
207	
208	### Layer 6 — Clinical Trial Simulation
209	
210	Disease progression in the absence of treatment is modeled as a stochastic differential equation, with drift and diffusion terms informed by longitudinal data from DCCT/EDIC and similar natural history cohorts. Trial simulations draw random samples from this virtual population, apply the PK/PD model for a proposed dose regimen, and propagate effects through the mechanistic layers to predict changes in primary endpoints — typically total neuropathy score, nerve conduction studies, or intraepidermal nerve fiber density. Bayesian adaptive trial designs can be explored in silico, optimizing interim decision rules before a single patient is enrolled.
211	
212	Critically, the clinical-trial layer feeds back to calibrate all layers below it. When a real trial produces a result, Bayes' theorem updates the joint posterior of every parameter in the system — tightening some distributions, sometimes forcing revision of mechanistic assumptions (as happened when AR inhibitors failed despite seemingly adequate target engagement). This is where the system learns from clinical reality rather than only from bench data.
213	
214	---
215	
216	## Integration Architecture: A Probabilistic Knowledge Graph
217	
218	Knitting these six layers together is a probabilistic knowledge graph — a directed graph (with feedback loops across layers) in which nodes represent biological entities (metabolites, genes, proteins, cell types, clinical endpoints) and edges represent mechanistic or regulatory relationships with posterior probability distributions on their parameters.
219	
220	This graph is the system's "memory." It is populated initially by automated extraction from the biomedical literature using large language models fine-tuned on pharmacology and neuroscience text, with human expert curation validating extracted relationships. Every relationship in the graph carries provenance: which papers, which experiments, which species, what quality of evidence. Conflicting evidence is represented explicitly as multimodal posteriors rather than forced into a single consensus. When new experimental data arrive — from an in-house assay, a published study, or a clinical trial — a Bayesian update engine propagates the information through the graph, revising downstream distributions accordingly.
221	
222	Active experimental design is built in from the start. Given current parameter uncertainties, the system can compute which experiment — which enzyme kinetics assay, which animal study endpoint, which patient biomarker — would most reduce uncertainty in a specified clinical prediction. This transforms the system from a passive repository into a scientific collaborator that recommends where to invest next.
223	
224	---
225	
226	## Practical Considerations and Known Challenges
227	
228	Several challenges deserve honest acknowledgment. Cross-species translation is the most treacherous step: the posteriors on human regulatory network parameters will remain broad for a long time, because direct human peripheral nerve biochemistry data are scarce and ethically constrained. The system must be designed to represent this ignorance faithfully and to avoid overconfident clinical predictions.
229	
230	Model identifiability is a constant concern — many parameter combinations may fit available data equally well, and the system must use hierarchical priors and regularization rather than allowing unconstrained inference. Computational cost of full Bayesian inference across five coupled layers requires careful approximation strategies: variational inference, sequential Monte Carlo, and emulator-based approaches all have roles to play.
231	
232	Finally, the system must be governable by scientists who are not Bayesian statisticians. A well-designed interface layer — translating posterior distributions into intuitive visualizations, flagging high-uncertainty predictions, and explaining the evidence chain behind any conclusion — is as important as the mathematical machinery underneath.
233	
234	---
235	
236	## Summary
237	
238	What this system ultimately offers is not a replacement for scientific judgment but an amplifier of it: a way to make the full weight of accumulated biomedical knowledge bearing on diabetic neuropathy computationally tractable, consistently updated, and honest about what we know versus what we are guessing. That combination of mechanism, uncertainty, and continuous learning is what distinguishes it from both static pathway databases and opaque machine learning models.
239	
240	---
241	
242	# Utility of the Approach: Applications and Capabilities
243	
244	The core utility is **causal, mechanistic extrapolation under quantified uncertainty** — something neither pure machine learning nor any single-scale model can offer. Most existing tools answer questions about situations already observed. This system is designed to answer questions about situations not yet encountered, by reasoning from first principles through a connected chain of mechanism. Below are the domains of utility, illustrated with concrete examples.
245	
246	---
247	
248	## Diagnosing Historical Failures
249	
250	Perhaps the most immediate and humbling application is retrospective: understanding why aldose reductase inhibitors, despite overwhelming preclinical rationale and decades of investment, produced a nearly unbroken record of clinical failures. The system would be calibrated against this history as a mandatory prior to any forward prediction.
251	
252	Working backward from null trial results, the Bayesian update engine would interrogate which mechanistic assumptions were most inconsistent with observed outcomes. Candidate explanations include insufficient nerve tissue penetration (the PK/PD layer), species differences in the ratio of AR-dependent to AR-independent glucose flux (the GRN layer), patient populations with HbA1c too variable to maintain stable pathway activation during a trial (the clinical layer), or primary endpoints too insensitive to detect early reversal of fiber loss. Crucially, these hypotheses are not mutually exclusive and the system does not force a single answer — it returns a posterior probability over explanations. This is qualitatively different from a post-hoc narrative, because it produces quantitative predictions: "if the failure was primarily due to insufficient tissue exposure, then an improved formulation achieving X-fold higher nerve Cmax should produce Y% improvement in nerve conduction velocity in Z% of patients."
253	
254	No existing method — literature review, empirical modeling, or standard PK/PD — can do this in an integrated, probabilistically honest way.
255	
256	---
257	
258	## Rational Patient Stratification Before a Trial Begins
259	
260	One of the most consequential and underappreciated causes of clinical failure in diabetic neuropathy trials is patient heterogeneity. A drug that mechanistically should work in patients with high polyol pathway flux may be diluted into statistical noise by enrollment of patients whose neuropathy is driven primarily by inflammatory or ischemic mechanisms.
261	
262	The system addresses this directly. Because the GRN layer incorporates known genetic variants affecting AKR1B1 expression and enzyme function, it can generate a prior on each patient's expected pathway flux given their genotype, HbA1c history, and disease duration. The clinical layer then translates this into a predicted treatment effect size for that individual. The result is a prospectively defined enrichment biomarker — a computable patient selection criterion — derived not from a fishing expedition in trial data but from the mechanistic model.
263	
264	This is not attainable with existing approaches. Empirical ML-based patient stratification requires large historical trial datasets with the relevant biomarkers already measured, and even then produces black-box subgroup definitions. The mechanistic system can propose stratification criteria for a drug mechanism that has never succeeded in a trial, grounded in the biological logic of why those patients should respond.
265	
266	---
267	
268	## Combination Therapy Design Before Animal Studies
269	
270	Suppose a medicinal chemist proposes pairing an AR inhibitor with a NRF2 activator, reasoning that addressing both the sorbitol accumulation and the oxidative stress arms simultaneously might succeed where monotherapy failed. The question is whether this combination is synergistic, additive, or actually counterproductive (since NRF2 activation can upregulate AR expression in some contexts).
271	
272	The system can simulate this in silico. The AR inhibitor is represented as a fractional inhibition term on the Layer 1 kinetic model; the NRF2 activator modifies the regulatory network in Layer 2, altering expression of antioxidant genes and — via the GRN model — potentially feeding back on AKR1B1 transcription. The joint effect propagates through Layers 3–5, and the output is a credible interval on the combination's predicted clinical effect relative to each monotherapy, along with a sensitivity analysis identifying which mechanistic uncertainties most affect the synergy conclusion.
273	
274	This kind of multi-drug mechanistic simulation cannot be done with standard pharmacometric tools, which lack the biological substrate to reason about pathway-level interactions. Animal studies remain necessary for validation, but the system prioritizes which combinations are worth the investment and predicts the dose ratios most likely to produce synergy — dramatically narrowing the experimental space.
275	
276	---
277	
278	## Biomarker Discovery and Surrogate Endpoint Validation
279	
280	A persistent problem in neuropathy drug development is that primary endpoints — nerve conduction velocity, total neuropathy score — change slowly and require large, long trials to detect treatment effects. There is great interest in surrogate or early endpoints, but regulatory acceptance requires evidence that the surrogate captures the relevant biology.
281	
282	The knowledge system directly supports this. By computing, for each candidate biomarker (plasma sorbitol, skin punch biopsy nerve fiber density, corneal confocal microscopy metrics, serum neurofilament light chain), the mutual information with the clinical endpoint across the virtual patient population, the system ranks biomarkers by their mechanistic coupling to downstream outcomes. It can also identify conditions under which a biomarker decouples from the endpoint — for instance, if a drug reduces sorbitol but leaves the oxidative stress arm unaddressed, plasma sorbitol may improve while neurodegeneration continues, which would disqualify it as a reliable surrogate for that mechanism. This kind of biomarker qualification argument, grounded in explicit mechanism, is qualitatively more compelling to regulators than an empirical correlation in a single dataset.
283	
284	---
285	
286	## Adaptive Trial Design Optimization
287	
288	Before a trial is designed, the system runs tens of thousands of simulated trials varying the adaptive decision rules: when to look at interim data, what the stopping boundaries are, how to re-estimate sample size based on observed variance. Because the virtual patients are generated from a mechanistic model rather than a parametric statistical assumption, the simulated trials capture biologically realistic heterogeneity and non-linear treatment response trajectories.
289	
290	The output is not just operating characteristics (type I error, power) under a single assumed treatment effect, but a full posterior distribution over operating characteristics that reflects genuine uncertainty about the drug's mechanism. A trial design that looks well-powered under an optimistic mechanistic assumption but collapses under a more conservative one is identified before a single patient is enrolled — rather than discovered in a futility analysis.
291	
292	---
293	
294	## Active Experimental Design: Telling the Lab What to Measure
295	
296	This is perhaps the most operationally distinctive capability. At any point, a scientist can query the system: "Given our current state of knowledge, which experiment would most reduce our uncertainty about whether this drug will achieve a 3-point improvement in total neuropathy score at 52 weeks?"
297	
298	The system answers by computing the expected information gain from each feasible experiment — an in vitro Km determination, a rat nerve sorbitol measurement, a 13-week dog toxicology study with nerve biopsy, a phase II biomarker substudy. It returns a ranked list with quantitative justification. This transforms the experimental program from "run the standard assay battery" to a focused, decision-theoretic sequence of experiments, each chosen because it addresses the most consequential current uncertainty. In a development program where each study costs millions of dollars and months of time, this prioritization has enormous practical value.
299	
300	---
301	
302	## New Target Identification from the Knowledge Graph
303	
304	The probabilistic knowledge graph can be queried in a direction that no existing database supports: "Which nodes, if perturbed, would have the highest expected impact on nerve conduction velocity in a patient with moderate diabetic neuropathy, while having the lowest mechanistic coupling to nodes associated with known toxicities?" This is a graph-theoretic optimization problem over the posterior distributions of edge weights — essentially a computational target identification engine that reasons about mechanism, not just network topology.
305	
306	A query like this might surface, for example, a regulatory node governing both AGE formation and mitochondrial biogenesis that existing AR-centric thinking had not prioritized, or a microRNA governing Schwann cell remyelination whose expression is modulated by the hexosamine pathway branch. These hypotheses emerge from the system's integrated view across scales in a way that no single-scale analysis — transcriptomics alone, proteomics alone, metabolomics alone — could produce.
307	
308	---
309	
310	## Where Existing Methods Fall Short
311	
312	To make the contrast concrete: static pathway databases like KEGG or Reactome capture topology but not dynamics, carry no uncertainty, and cannot be updated from data. Standard machine learning models find correlations but cannot extrapolate mechanistically to unseen drug mechanisms or patient populations, and cannot simulate counterfactuals. Traditional pharmacometric models connect dose to clinical response but lack the biological substrate to reason about why a drug works, what patient characteristics predict response, or how a novel mechanism would behave. Animal models provide causal evidence but cannot answer questions about human-specific biology or clinical trial design. Each of these tools is valuable within its domain; what they cannot do individually or in combination is reason coherently across the full causal chain from enzyme kinetics to trial outcome, with uncertainty quantified at every step.
313	
314	That connected, probabilistic, multi-scale causal chain is what this system is designed to be.
315	
316	---
317	
318	# Pathway Analysis: Rate Control, Enzyme Quantities, and Pharmaceutical Amenability
319	
320	The system is purpose-built to answer mechanistic questions about the polyol pathway itself — which components are rate-limiting, how much enzyme is present in individual cells, what degree of modulation is needed to produce a therapeutic effect, and which targets are most amenable to pharmaceutical intervention. These questions sit at the interface of Layers 1 through 3 and illustrate why a mechanistic model with probability distributions on parameters is so much more powerful than either a static pathway diagram or a purely empirical approach.
321	
322	---
323	
324	## Which Components Are Rate-Limiting?
325	
326	"Rate-limiting" is not a binary property of an enzyme — it is a continuous, condition-dependent quantity, and the system makes this explicit. The formal mathematical framework for this is **Metabolic Control Analysis (MCA)**, and it is embedded directly into the Layer 1 ODE model.
327	
328	MCA defines a *flux control coefficient* (FCC) for each enzyme in a pathway: the fractional change in steady-state flux produced by a fractional change in that enzyme's activity. An FCC of 1.0 means the enzyme has complete control over flux; an FCC of 0.0 means it has none. Importantly, the FCCs of all enzymes in a pathway sum to 1.0, so control is shared, not monopolized, and the distribution of control shifts as conditions change.
329	
330	For the polyol pathway under normal glycemia, aldose reductase has a relatively high Km for glucose (approximately 50–100 mM by many estimates), meaning it is far below saturation and its activity is low. In this regime, the system is not under meaningful flux, and the concept of rate-limitation is almost moot. Under hyperglycemia, as intracellular glucose rises, AR becomes increasingly active. The FCC of AR increases substantially — it becomes more controlling — while cofactor availability begins to matter. Specifically, NADPH becomes a competitor for multiple pathways simultaneously (glutathione reductase, thioredoxin reductase, nitric oxide synthase, fatty acid synthesis), so the effective rate limitation may shift from the enzyme itself to NADPH supply, depending on the cellular context.
331	
332	Sorbitol dehydrogenase (SORD) introduces a second locus of control. If SORD is slower than AR under a given condition, sorbitol accumulates osmotically — the signature of early polyol pathway toxicity. If SORD is faster, the downstream fructose and NADH accumulation dominate. The system computes the FCC of each enzyme as a function of glucose concentration, NADPH availability, and enzyme expression level, returning not a single answer but a curve over the relevant physiological range, with credible intervals reflecting parameter uncertainty. This immediately tells a medicinal chemist whether inhibiting AR will reduce total pathway flux proportionally, or whether SORD or cofactor supply will simply become the new bottleneck.
333	
334	---
335	
336	## What Is the Quantity of Each Enzyme in Individual Cells?
337	
338	This is one of the hardest and most important questions in the field, and the system is designed to represent honestly how much and how little we know about it.
339	
340	The peripheral nervous system is not a uniform tissue. The relevant cell types — dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons, Schwann cells, endoneurial fibroblasts, and the endothelial cells of the vasa nervorum — express AR, SORD, and their regulators at very different levels, and these differences have direct consequences for which cell types are most damaged and which are most tractable as drug targets. A Schwann cell and a large myelinated sensory neuron may be bathed in the same hyperglycemic environment but have very different intracellular glucose concentrations, NADPH pools, and enzyme expression levels.
341	
342	The system integrates several data types to construct cell-type-specific enzyme quantity distributions. Bulk proteomics (mass spectrometry-based absolute protein quantification from nerve homogenates) provides a tissue-level prior. Single-cell RNA sequencing from DRG and peripheral nerve preparations — increasingly available in both rodent and human post-mortem tissue — provides cell-type-resolved expression estimates, with the important caveat that mRNA and protein abundance correlate imperfectly. Cell-type-specific immunofluorescence quantification (confocal microscopy with calibrated standard curves) provides a third, orthogonal data source. A hierarchical Bayesian model reconciles these three sources, weighting them by their respective measurement uncertainties, and returns a posterior distribution on protein copy number per cell for each cell type.
343	
344	The resulting estimates carry substantial uncertainty — especially for human tissue, where biopsy availability is limited and post-mortem RNA quality is variable. But crucially, the system does not hide this uncertainty behind a point estimate. It reports it explicitly, and the downstream sensitivity analyses automatically propagate it: if we are unsure whether DRG neurons express 10,000 or 100,000 AR molecules per cell, the uncertainty in the predicted therapeutic effect of an AR inhibitor in those neurons is correspondingly large, and the system flags this as a priority for experimental resolution.
345	
346	---
347	
348	## To What Extent Must Enzyme Quantity or Activity Be Changed to Impact the System?
349	
350	This is the question of **therapeutic threshold**, and it is where the mechanistic model provides insight that no amount of clinical correlation can replicate.
351	
352	The relationship between fractional enzyme inhibition and fractional reduction in pathway flux is almost never linear, for two reasons. First, most enzymes operate with significant *spare capacity* — they are present in excess of what is needed to sustain flux at the prevailing substrate concentration, particularly for enzymes with high Km operating below substrate saturation. For such an enzyme, inhibiting 50% of activity may reduce flux by far less than 50%, because the remaining enzyme can compensate by operating closer to its Vmax. Second, upstream metabolites may accumulate when downstream enzymes are inhibited, relieving substrate saturation at the inhibited step in a self-correcting loop.
353	
354	The system computes this relationship explicitly. For AR, it produces a curve relating fractional inhibition (from 0% to 100%) to fractional change in sorbitol accumulation, NADPH depletion, and — propagating through Layers 2 and 3 — eventual change in nerve conduction velocity. This curve typically shows a threshold region where moderate inhibition has little effect, followed by a steep zone where efficacy emerges, followed potentially by a plateau where further inhibition yields diminishing returns. The location and steepness of these transitions depend critically on the parameters that carry the most uncertainty: intracellular glucose concentration in the relevant cell type, basal NADPH turnover, and the competing demands on NADPH from other enzymes.
355	
356	This analysis has direct clinical and chemical consequences. It tells the medicinal chemist what degree of target engagement is actually needed — not just "more is better" — and it explains why an AR inhibitor that achieves 70% inhibition in a plasma binding assay but only 30% inhibition in peripheral nerve tissue may sit entirely below the therapeutic threshold. It also identifies whether there is a *ceiling effect*: beyond some level of pathway inhibition, the downstream damage is driven by other mechanisms (AGE formation, PKC activation, hexosamine flux) that AR inhibition does not address, and incremental AR inhibition yields no further clinical benefit. This ceiling is not a conjecture — it is a calculated feature of the multi-pathway model, and it has direct implications for combination therapy design.
357	
358	---
359	
360	## Which Components Are Most Amenable to Pharmaceutical Intervention?
361	
362	This is the synthesis of the preceding three questions, and it is where the system's integrated, multi-scale architecture pays its greatest dividend.
363	
364	Pharmaceutical amenability has at least four independent dimensions: (1) how much control the target exerts over the relevant downstream pathology (the FCC question); (2) what degree of modulation is needed to cross the therapeutic threshold (the inhibition-response question); (3) whether the target is structurally tractable for drug design (druggability, assessed from structural databases and prior medicinal chemistry); and (4) what the selectivity landscape looks like — how similar the target is to other enzymes in the same family whose inhibition would cause off-target toxicity.
365	
366	The system addresses all four. AR itself scores well on control and druggability — its active site is well-characterized — but scores poorly on selectivity (the aldo-keto reductase family is large and the active sites are similar, creating toxicity risks) and on the therapeutic threshold question in humans (the historical trials suggest the threshold is higher than previously appreciated, possibly because nerve tissue exposure was insufficient). SORD, by contrast, has a higher FCC under conditions of sorbitol accumulation but has received far less medicinal chemistry attention, and its structural druggability is less well characterized — a gap the system would flag as warranting investment.
367	
368	Beyond the two primary enzymes, the system evaluates all nodes that influence polyol pathway flux, including the glucose transporters that determine intracellular glucose concentration (themselves regulated by insulin signaling), the enzymes competing for NADPH, and the transcriptional regulators that set basal AR expression level. A transcriptional approach — epigenetically silencing AKR1B1 expression rather than inhibiting the enzyme's activity — would shift the dose-response relationship entirely, because reducing enzyme quantity changes the system's spare capacity and lowers the effective threshold for pathway suppression. This is not a hypothesis the system generates from speculation; it is a quantitative prediction that follows directly from the MCA framework, and it suggests a therapeutic modality that has received essentially no attention in the AR inhibitor literature.
369
```
</details></tool-use>

17	## The Governing Philosophy: Mechanistic Skeleton, Bayesian Flesh, and Graph Relationship Map
18	
19	The foundational design principle is that **every layer of the system is a mechanistic model with probability distributions on its parameters, not a black box**. Machine learning enters not to replace mechanism but to (a) extract and encode knowledge from literature and experiments, (b) serve as fast surrogates for expensive simulations, and (c) update parameter distributions as new evidence arrives. The result is a living, self-updating scientific belief system rather than a static model.
20	
21	Uncertainty is not an afterthought — it propagates upward through every layer, so that clinical predictions carry honest credible intervals that trace back to our ignorance about, say, a particular enzyme's Km in human sural nerve tissue.
22	
23	The relationships among all models — within layers and across layers — are captured in a **graph relationship map**. This is explicitly *not* a directed acyclic graph (DAG): the system contains feedback loops. Posterior updates from clinical outcomes propagate back to refine pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic parameters; tissue-level pathology constrains the gene-regulatory priors; virtual patient behavior feeds back into the biochemical kinetics of the next simulation cycle. A DAG cannot represent these cycles. The graph relationship map therefore uses a general directed graph, where nodes are model bundles and edges encode directional influence. This map serves as the connective tissue of the entire architecture: it determines which inferences must be recomputed when new evidence arrives, and it keeps the mechanistic structure explicit and auditable rather than buried in software dependencies.
24	
25	---
26	
27	## Conceptual Diagrams
28	
29	The figures below summarize the architecture before the text walks through each layer in detail. The first shows the six-resolution stack, with biochemical kinetics at the bottom and trial simulation at the top. The next three diagrams zoom in on inter-model connectivity, the structure of a single model bundle, and the continuous evidence-to-posterior update loop. They are rendered as plain-text Unicode diagrams so they remain stable across Markdown viewers.

220	Knitting these six layers together is a probabilistic knowledge graph — a directed graph (with feedback loops across layers) in which nodes represent biological entities (metabolites, genes, proteins, cell types, clinical endpoints) and edges represent mechanistic or regulatory relationships with posterior probability distributions on their parameters.

When new experimental data arrive — from an in-house assay, a published study, or a clinical trial — a Bayesian update engine propagates the information through the graph, revising downstream distributions accordingly.
223	
224	Active experimental design is built in from the start. Given current parameter uncertainties, the system can compute which experiment — which enzyme kinetics assay, which animal study endpoint, which patient biomarker — would most reduce uncertainty in a specified clinical prediction. This transforms the system from a passive repository into a scientific collaborator that recommends where to invest next.

227	
228	## Practical Considerations and Known Challenges
229	
230	Several challenges deserve honest acknowledgment. Cross-species translation is the most treacherous step: the posteriors on human regulatory network parameters will remain broad for a long time, because direct human peripheral nerve biochemistry data are scarce and ethically constrained. The system must be designed to represent this ignorance faithfully and to avoid overconfident clinical predictions.
231	
232	Model identifiability is a constant concern — many parameter combinations may fit available data equally well, and the system must use hierarchical priors and regularization rather than allowing unconstrained inference. Computational cost of full Bayesian inference across five coupled layers requires careful approximation strategies: variational inference, sequential Monte Carlo, and emulator-based approaches all have roles to play.
233	
234	Finally, the system must be governable by scientists who are not Bayesian statisticians. A well-designed interface layer — translating posterior distributions into intuitive visualizations, flagging high-uncertainty predictions, and explaining the evidence chain behind any conclusion — is as important as the mathematical machinery underneath.
```
</details></tool-use>

1	# An AI-Driven Mechanistic Knowledge System for Diabetic Neuropathy
2	
3	**Last Updated:** 2026-04-14 EDT
4	
5	**Executive Summary:** This document proposes a multi-resolution, mechanistic, Bayesian knowledge system for diabetic neuropathy that links biochemical kinetics, gene regulation, tissue pathophysiology, pharmacology, virtual patient generation, and trial simulation. The architecture is designed to support causal reasoning, uncertainty propagation, adaptive updating from new evidence, and practical decision support for biomarker discovery, trial design, and target prioritization.
6	
7	## Contents
8	- [The Governing Philosophy: Mechanistic Skeleton, Bayesian Ontological Sinew, Bayesian Muscle](#the-governing-philosophy-mechanistic-skeleton-bayesian-ontological-sinew-bayesian-muscle)
9	- [Conceptual Diagrams](#conceptual-diagrams)
10	- [Layered Architecture](#layered-architecture)
11	- [Integration Architecture: A Probabilistic Ontology](#integration-architecture-a-probabilistic-ontology)
12	- [Practical Considerations and Known Challenges](#practical-considerations-and-known-challenges)
13	- [Summary](#summary)
14	- [Utility of the Approach: Applications and Capabilities](#utility-of-the-approach-applications-and-capabilities)
15	- [Pathway Analysis: Rate Control, Enzyme Quantities, and Pharmaceutical Amenability](#pathway-analysis-rate-control-enzyme-quantities-and-pharmaceutical-amenability)
16	
17	## The Governing Philosophy: Mechanistic Skeleton, Bayesian Ontological Sinew, Bayesian Muscle
18	
19	The architecture rests on three interlocking elements whose roles are captured by an anatomical metaphor.
20	
21	**Mechanistic skeleton.** Every layer of the system is a mechanistic model — ODEs for biochemical kinetics, stochastic regulatory networks, PK/PD equations, compartmental tissue models — whose structure is derived from first principles, not learned from data. This is the load-bearing frame. It prevents the system from collapsing into a correlation engine when extrapolating to drug mechanisms or patient populations never before observed. Machine learning enters not to replace mechanism but to (a) extract and encode knowledge from literature and experiments, (b) serve as fast surrogates for expensive simulations, and (c) propose updates to parameter distributions as new evidence arrives.
22	
23	**Bayesian ontological sinew.** Just as sinew anchors muscle to bone and transmits contractile force into structured movement, the **probabilistic ontology** anchors Bayesian inference to the mechanistic skeleton and transmits posterior updates into structured revision of scientific belief. The ontology is a formally defined vocabulary of biological concepts — metabolites, enzymes, cell types, clinical endpoints — and their directional, quantified relationships, each edge carrying a posterior probability distribution on its parameters. This is explicitly *not* a directed acyclic graph (DAG): the system contains feedback loops. Posterior updates from clinical outcomes propagate back to refine pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic parameters; tissue-level pathology constrains the gene-regulatory priors; virtual patient behavior feeds back into the biochemical kinetics of the next simulation cycle. The ontology therefore uses a general directed graph where ontological classes are model bundles and properties are quantified, directional influences. It determines which inferences must be recomputed when new evidence arrives, and keeps the knowledge structure auditable rather than buried in software dependencies.
24	
25	**Bayesian muscle.** Uncertainty is not an afterthought — it propagates upward through every layer, so that clinical predictions carry honest credible intervals that trace all the way back to our ignorance about, say, a particular enzyme's Km in human sural nerve tissue. When new experimental data arrive, Bayesian inference contracts through the ontological sinew, updating the joint posterior of every parameter the evidence touches and propagating the revision outward to all downstream inferences. This active, force-generating updating is what animates the system: a living, self-revising scientific belief machine rather than a static compendium.
26	
27	---
28

30	
31	The figures below summarize the architecture before the text walks through each layer in detail. The first shows the six-resolution stack, with biochemical kinetics at the bottom and trial simulation at the top. The next three diagrams zoom in on inter-model connectivity, the structure of a single model bundle, and the continuous evidence-to-posterior update loop. They are rendered as plain-text Unicode diagrams so they remain stable across Markdown viewers.

155	
156	## Layered Architecture
157	
158	### Layer 1 — The Biochemical Core: Polyol Pathway Kinetics
159	
160	At the finest resolution, we build a fully parameterized ordinary differential equation model of the polyol pathway and its immediate consequences. Glucose enters via the aldose reductase (AKR1B1) reaction, producing sorbitol at the cost of NADPH; sorbitol dehydrogenase then oxidizes sorbitol to fructose at the cost of NAD⁺. These two reactions are the beating heart of the system, and their kinetics — Michaelis constants, catalytic rates, inhibition constants — are encoded as probability distributions, not point estimates.
161	
162	The model's state variables include intracellular glucose, sorbitol, fructose, NADPH/NADP⁺ ratio, and NAD⁺/NADH ratio. From these we derive downstream consequences that link to the next layer: depletion of NADPH starves glutathione reductase, reducing the GSH/GSSG ratio and driving oxidative stress; NADH accumulation feeds pseudohypoxia; elevated fructose fuels the hexosamine pathway and advanced glycation end-product (AGE) formation; and diacylglycerol accumulation activates protein kinase C isoforms. Each of these is itself a small mechanistic sub-module with its own parameterization.
163	
164	Bayesian priors for this layer come from decades of in vitro enzyme kinetics literature — Km and Vmax measured in crystallographic and biochemical studies, inhibition constants from aldose reductase inhibitor programs, and intracellular metabolite concentrations from isotope tracing experiments. A literature-mining AI agent (a fine-tuned large language model with structured extraction) continuously reads new papers and proposes updates to these priors, flagged for human scientist review before incorporation.
165	
166	---
167	
168	### Layer 2 — Gene Regulatory Networks: From Model Organisms to Humans
169	
170	The biochemical layer tells us what the pathway does given fixed enzyme levels, but gene expression is itself regulated and varies across individuals, tissues, and species. The second layer is a probabilistic gene regulatory network (GRN) model governing the expression of AKR1B1, SORD, and their transcriptional regulators — SP1, NF-κB, NRF2, and osmotic response element binding protein (OREBP/TonEBP), among others.
171	
172	In model organisms — primarily the streptozotocin rat and the db/db mouse — we have rich time-series transcriptomic data from sciatic and sural nerves under hyperglycemia, with and without aldose reductase inhibitor treatment. A Bayesian network learning algorithm (using a variant of the PC algorithm with Bayesian scoring) infers regulatory edges and assigns posterior probabilities to their existence and direction. The parameters of these regulatory relationships are themselves distributions, updated as new animal data arrive.
173	
174	The critical and most scientifically demanding step is species translation. Rodent and human AR gene promoters differ substantially; human GWAS and eQTL data from diabetic neuropathy cohorts (the DCCT/EDIC biorepository, UK Biobank, and others) are integrated as a separate data source. A hierarchical Bayesian model treats the rodent GRN and the human GRN as related but distinct, sharing structural priors while allowing divergence. Posterior inference on the human regulatory network is therefore informed by the richer rodent data but appropriately discounted. Genetic variants affecting AKR1B1 expression or enzyme function enter as modifiers of the prior, enabling patient stratification.
175	
176	---
177	
178	### Layer 3 — Cellular and Tissue Pathophysiology: The Neuron and Its Environment
179	
180	Peripheral sensory and motor neurons in diabetic neuropathy are damaged through a confluence of mechanisms that the polyol pathway feeds: oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired axonal transport, Schwann cell dysfunction, and endoneurial microvascular ischemia. Layer 3 translates the biochemical outputs of Layers 1–2 into cellular and tissue-level phenomena.
181	
182	Here we use a combination of mechanistic compartmental models and partial differential equations. Axonal transport is modeled as a reaction-diffusion system, with polyol pathway-driven ATP depletion and oxidative modification of kinesin/dynein motors entering as degradation terms — their magnitudes drawn from the distributions established in Layers 1 and 2. Mitochondrial membrane potential dynamics follow established biophysical frameworks (loosely in the Nicholls tradition), with ROS production coupled to the NADH/NAD⁺ imbalance from Layer 1. Nerve conduction velocity is an emergent output, computed from Hodgkin-Huxley-style cable models of myelinated axons with Schwann cell geometry parameterized from morphometric data in rodent and human nerve biopsy studies.
183	
184	Endoneurial blood flow is modeled as a separate but coupled sub-system: AGEs cross-link basement membrane components, nitric oxide synthesis is impaired through NADPH depletion, and the resulting ischemia feeds back on axonal oxygen availability. The coupling between vascular and neural sub-models is one of the richest sources of non-linearity — and therefore one of the most important contributors to uncertainty in downstream predictions.
185	
186	Because full simulation of this layer is computationally expensive, we train deep neural network surrogate models (emulators) that accept the parameter distributions from Layers 1–2 as inputs and return fast approximations of Layer 3 outputs with calibrated uncertainty. These emulators are retrained as new mechanistic simulations are run, in an active learning loop that prioritizes the parameter regions most relevant to clinical interventions being evaluated.
